prompt_en: A documentary photograph in a small lampworking studio on a rainy evening, following a female glassmaker as she completes the missing central bead for an unfinished glass necklace. Her face, black chin-length bob and wispy bangs follow the supplied reference photograph. Her quiet concentration has a warm, approachable presence: her lips rest slightly parted and her eyes follow the glass rather than the camera. In this moment she heats a glass bead with a flame. A bench-mounted brass gas torch sits firmly on the fireproof work surface in front of her. A visible flame supplies heat: one narrow blue jet issues directly from its round nozzle, with a pale-blue inner cone surrounded by a translucent deeper-blue outer flame. A strip of dark workshop air on either side makes the gently tapered flame edge readable right down to its continuous base at the brass nozzle. The blue flame envelope is rooted at the burner mouth, while the warm brass burner and matte graphite paddle retain their separate material colors. The flame points diagonally upward and reaches the underside of a small glass bead on a horizontal steel mandrel. The bead has a brilliant orange heated center fading into dark translucent amber at its edges; the blue flame remains a separate visible shape beside this incandescent glass. She rolls the cool end of the mandrel between her right thumb and index finger, keeping the rod level while its hot bead stays at the flame tip. Her left hand holds a flat black graphite paddle beside the bead, paused beyond the flame's edge for the next shaping step. Both hands, the unbroken mandrel, the nozzle and the flame-to-glass gap appear together. Her elbows stay near her torso and her shoulders remain relaxed behind the bench. A shallow ceramic tray set aside from the hot work holds cool amber-and-teal beads, a partly assembled necklace with an empty central position, and one cracked practice bead. These glass pieces look solid and reflective while the heated bead still glows. A charcoal work apron over a faded teal shirt carries small scorch marks and glass dust. Cool rain streaks on the workshop window soften the background; the restrained warm sheen on her cheek and knuckles belongs to the hot work. Photograph from an oblique position across the bench, at chest height, in a horizontal environmental portrait with enough depth of field to show her attentive face and the working relationship below it. Preserve textured skin, graphite wear, tool scratches, and clear glass edges. The first visual pull is the small flame and bead; her absorbed expression and the necklace gap explain why this delicate moment matters.
